https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/world-news.text: The world as we know it is about to change. The United Nations has voted to retire the world map. Yep, the commonly used world map used in classrooms, government buildings, and on globes worldwide. Instead, a new map will be endorsed which will see the United States shrink and Africa increase in size. So why has the UN chosen to ditch our centuries-old, beloved world map? It all comes down to design, with a 2018 design called the Equal Earth projection now found to be a more accurate representation of what our world actually looks like. It corrects scale and layout issues that have distorted our world view for more than 450 years thanks to geographical and geometrical warping caused by Mercator, the original world map designer. Mercator's map artificially stretches land masses as they get further away from the equator. Basically, it has been distorting some nations and shrinking others for centuries. Take the United States and Greenland as an example. On a Mercator map, the two nations look to be the same size. But, in reality, Greenland is about 14 times larger in landmass compared to America. It is impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart, so whenever a map of the world gets drawn up, sacrifices have to be made. Mercator aimed to preserve direction in order to help explorers fan out in ships to explore the world. So, at the expense of area, land masses must become enlarged the further they are from the equator to account for the Earth's curvature. As the new design corrects these spatial exaggerations, the US will be shrunken down on new maps going forward, while continents like Africa and Australia will look vastly larger. At the UN General Assembly, a resolution was put forward by a coalition of African nations calling for our world maps to stop minimising their continent. It proposed the UN endorse the updated map designs, with a total of 164 countries voting in agreement on Friday (September 4). The resolution was passed, and the UN will now recommend the new world map design to ensure maps "more accurately reflect the true size" of our world. Six countries – Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia, and Ukraine – abstained from voting at the UN General Assembly, while one lone dissenting voice opposed the new map design: the United States of America. With the US set to shrink under new map designs, it would seem that perhaps size does matter. But if that were the motivation behind America's 'no' vote, they weren't letting it on. Instead, Washington's representative accused the UN-approved map resolution of being about much more than just correcting map proportions. “This resolution mocks the work and purpose of this institution,” US representative to the UN Yaryna Ferencevych, dubbing the "Correct the Map" vote as part of a wider “radical ideological project“ that undermines "common sense" global policies. In a statement explaining its reason to vote no, the US slammed the UN for "debating map projects from the 16th century" instead of real-world issues like "international peace, prosperity, or good relations". Diplomats from Togo led the campaign to get the new map vote before the broader UN General Assembly. The nation's foreign minister, Robert Dussey, pointed out that maps are far more symbolic than people give them credit for. “A fair map does not change the geography of the world; it changes how we see the world,” he said. France, another nation set to shrink on the new proposed map designs, issued a statement of its own prior to the UN vote. French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot confirmed Paris will nix the Mercator chart in favour of the Equal Earth projection. As for Mercator, his maps won't just vanish from circulation, as the UN resolution is non-binding. Governments can choose to use either design, but the power of choice creates a new cartographic culture more focused on fairness and equality for all.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwgk.text: Figure caption, Watch Chris Pelkey's AI-rendered impact statement shown in court By Ana Faguy Published 4 hours ago An Arizona road rage killer will be resentenced after an appeals court ruled that an AI-generated video message from his dead victim was improperly aired in court. Gabriel Paul Horcasitas was found guilty by a jury of shooting and killing Christopher Pelkey, 37, during a confrontation at a red light in 2021. He was sentenced to 10 years behind bars. But his legal team appealed, arguing that the trial judge should not have allowed an AI video, created by Pelkey's family, to be shown in court ahead of last year's sentencing. The Arizona Court of Appeals agreed, ruling that Horcasitas, 55, must be resentenced because the AI clip "crossed that line". "Rather than document an event or recording a particular moment, the AI video presents a depiction of the victim and his thoughts created from the imaginings of the victim's sister," the court of appeals wrote on Wednesday. Horcasitas' lawyer, Kristen Reller, who filed the appeal, declined to comment. Jessica Gattuso, an attorney for victims in the case, did not respond to a request for comment. Pelkey's sister, Stacey Wales, told the BBC last year the family had used voice recordings, videos and pictures to recreate him for the AI video. "To Gabriel Horcasitas, the man who shot me, it is a shame we encountered each other that day in those circumstances," said the AI version of Pelkey in court in 2025. "In another life, we probably could have been friends." "I believe in forgiveness, and a God who forgives. I always have and I still do," the AI version of Pelkey - wearing a grey baseball cap - continued. At the time of the sentencing, the judge who oversaw the case, Todd Lang, seemed to appreciate the use of AI. "I loved that AI, thank you for that. As angry as you are, as justifiably angry as the family is, I heard the forgiveness," Judge Lang said. "I feel that that was genuine." StaceviÄius / LRT Lithuaniaâs parliament voted Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment that would remove a ban on weapons of mass destruction from the countryâs constitution, potentially opening the way for allied nuclear weapons to be stationed in Lithuania. The amendment passed its first reading with 106 lawmakers voting in favour, 18 against and six abstaining. A final vote cannot be held until at least three months after Tuesdayâs vote. The amendment will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of the Seimas to pass. Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas has said the final vote is scheduled for January 12. Olekas said before the vote that removing the ban would strengthen Lithuaniaâs resilience and deterrence capabilities. He said eliminating the restriction would also remove a legal distinction between Lithuania and other European Union and NATO countries. âWe will ensure stronger support that could be available to us,â Olekas said. âBy addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal.â Opposition conservative leader Laurynas KasÄiÅ«nas urged lawmakers to support the amendment, saying neighbouring countries do not have similar restrictions. He argued that the existing constitutional provision prevents NATO allies from fully including Lithuania in the allianceâs nuclear deterrence planning. âWith the current restriction, we cannot fully participate in NATOâs nuclear deterrence plans,â KasÄiÅ«nas said. âSince nuclear deterrence is the queen of deterrence as a whole, this decision is strategically important.â Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas also stressed the importance of deterrence, saying politicians should provide the country with every available tool to ensure its security. Kaunas said Lithuania is surrounded by countries with strategic weapons, pointing to Russiaâs Kaliningrad region and Belarus. He described the proposed constitutional change as a response to Moscowâs actions. âWe are responding to Russiaâs aggression,â Kaunas said. âIf Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions we are having today.â Article 137 of Lithuaniaâs Constitution currently states that weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases may not be stationed on Lithuanian territory. The proposed amendment would remove that provision. Opponents call for referendum The amendment faced its strongest opposition from lawmakers in the opposition Nemunas Dawn party. Fourteen party members voted against it and two abstained. Aidas Gedvilas of Nemunas Dawn said he was surprised that parliament considered itself empowered to make such a fundamental change and called for a referendum. âThere are certainly alternatives to this constitutional provision. We could resolve this through a referendum,â Gedvilas said. Three members of the mixed parliamentary group and one lawmaker from the Farmers and Greens Union and Christian Families Alliance also voted against the amendment. The debate comes amid broader discussions in Europe about strengthening nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron presented an idea in March for a new European nuclear deterrence framework under which partner countries could temporarily host Franceâs nuclear-capable strategic air forces. The Financial Times reported in June that the United States was considering deploying nuclear weapons in several additional NATO countries in Europe. Lithuanian military analysts have said Russian media has taken an interest in Lithuaniaâs plans to remove the constitutional ban. In early September, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned that Lithuania could become a target for Russia if it allowed allies to deploy nuclear weapons on its territory. Dmitry Peskov | AP Reactions from Moscow The Kremlin warned Tuesday that the deployment of nuclear weapons or a permanent US military base in Lithuania would constitute an escalation and force Russia to take measures to protect its security. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian state media. âA military base is part of military infrastructure. If someoneâs military infrastructure â in fact, that of a major NATO member â is approaching our borders, of course, this can only be viewed as a step toward escalation,â Peskov said at a news conference. âThe same applies to the deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of a neighbouring country,â he added. Peskov was asked how Moscow would respond if Lithuania moved to lift its constitutional ban on deploying nuclear weapons while the United States considered establishing a permanent base there. âAll this will not help ensure stability and predictability on the European continent,â Peskov said. âOn the contrary, to our regret, it would be another very significant escalation.â âAs for Russia, of course, Russia will have to take all necessary measures to guarantee its security,â he said. Lithuanian officials have stressed that there are currently no plans to deploy nuclear weapons in the country. They say removing the constitutional restriction is intended to ensure that Lithuania does not face legal obstacles to participating in NATOâs nuclear deterrence arrangements.
